q: What is the main difference between a Server Component and a Client Component rendered with SSR?
options: A Server Component produces HTML on the server, while SSR produces a JSON payload that the browser turns into HTML
Its code never reaches the browser; an SSR-rendered Client Component still ships its code to hydrate
SSR runs only once at build time, while Server Components run on every request and cannot be cached
Server Components cannot fetch data themselves, so SSR is still needed for every page that shows data
explain: SSR is about when HTML is produced; a Client Component rendered that way still sends its JavaScript so it can hydrate. A Server Component runs only on the server, at build or request time, and sends none. The first option inverts things: the RSC Payload is the serialised output of Server Components, and HTML comes from prerendering.

q: add-to-cart-button.tsx starts with 'use client' and imports formatPrice from lib/money.ts, which has no directive. Where does formatPrice end up?
options: Only on the server, because a module without a directive defaults to the server
It depends on whether formatPrice is async: async helpers always stay on the server
Nowhere: the build fails until lib/money.ts gets its own 'use client'
In the client bundle, because the directive covers everything the module imports
explain: React documents that 'use client' marks the module and its transitive dependencies as client code, so you do not repeat the directive in every helper. Having no directive does not keep a module on the server; only import 'server-only' would turn that import into a build error.

q: Which prop can the product page (a Server Component) pass to a Client Component?
options: A promise of the reviews, which the Client Component unwraps with use() inside a Suspense boundary
An onAddToCart arrow function defined in the page, which the button calls on click
A Product class instance, so the button can call product.formatPrice() itself
A Symbol('cart') created in the page, used as a stable identity for the cart
explain: Promises are in React's list of serialisable props, and Next.js documents passing an unawaited promise and reading it with use() under Suspense. Plain functions (other than Server Functions), class instances and symbols not registered with Symbol.for cannot cross the boundary.

q: The header and the price box both call getCurrentCustomer, wrapped with React.cache in a shared module. What does that guarantee?
options: The customer is cached across requests for as long as the session cookie is valid
The result is shared between all visitors until the next deploy invalidates it
Within one server request, components calling the same wrapped function share one call
The result is memoized in the browser too, so hydration does not fetch the customer again
explain: React clears the cache for each server request and shares it only among components that call the same memoized function during rendering. It is not a cross-request cache (that is 'use cache'), so the first two options are wrong, and it is for Server Components, not the browser.

q: A page renders a heading and a price inside <Suspense fallback="Loading price...">; the price resolves after 300 ms. What does renderToReadableStream send?
options: Nothing until the price resolves, then the whole page in a single chunk
The heading and the fallback first, then the price with a small swap script
The price first, because suspended content is sent with a higher priority than the shell
The complete page twice: once with the fallback and once more with the price
explain: Measured on React 19.3.1: the first chunk left at 58 ms with the heading and "Loading price...", the second at 305 ms with the price in a hidden element and the inline swap script. Waiting for everything is what non-streaming rendering would need; renderToString does not even wait and sends the fallback.

q: The server rendered "Delivered by Tuesday" and the first client render produces "Delivered by Wednesday". What did React 19.3.1 do (measured)?
options: It reported a recoverable error and rebuilt the tree on the client: Wednesday
It kept Tuesday silently: hydration ignores text differences
It threw an uncaught error, and the customer saw a blank page instead of the product
It patched only the text node to Wednesday, without reporting anything to monitoring
explain: Measured with hydrateRoot in jsdom: onRecoverableError received "Hydration failed because the server rendered text didn't match the client. As a result this tree will be regenerated on the client", and the DOM ended with the client text. Keeping the server text happens only with suppressHydrationWarning.

q: With Cache Components enabled, a component reads cookies() and is not inside any Suspense boundary. What happens?
options: cookies() returns an empty cookie store during prerendering, without any warning
The whole application silently switches to request-time rendering, page by page
Next.js caches it per visitor, keyed on the cookie
Next.js flags the route as blocking and asks you to add a Suspense boundary
explain: Cache Components requires runtime data to sit behind a Suspense boundary so every route keeps a static shell; the dev overlay shows the blocking-route insight and the build guides you to fix it. Returning empty values is what dynamic = 'force-static' does in the previous model, not this one.

q: In a Server Action, a customer updates their saved delivery address, and the page must show the new address in the same response. Which call?
options: revalidateTag('address-' + customer.id, 'max')
revalidatePath('/') from a Client Component
updateTag('address-' + customer.id)
cacheLife('seconds') on the address reader
explain: updateTag expires the tag immediately, for read-your-own-writes, and is reserved for Server Actions. revalidateTag with a profile is stale-while-revalidate: the action's own re-render does not wait for fresh data, so the customer could still see the old address.

q: Which statement about a Server Action exported from app/checkout/actions.ts is true?
options: Anyone able to send the POST can call it, so it must check the session, ownership and input itself
It is private, because Next.js encrypts action ids and removes the actions you do not use
The sign-in check in app/checkout/page.tsx protects it too, since the page renders the form
Only the form that imports it can call it, because Next.js compares Origin and Host
explain: Next.js documents that actions are reachable by direct POST requests and that a page-level check does not extend to the actions it renders. Encrypted ids and dead-code removal reduce exposure but are explicitly not a substitute for checks inside each action; the Origin check stops cross-site forms, not a direct request.

q: Where should ORDERS_API_CLIENT_SECRET live in the storefront?
options: NEXT_PUBLIC_ORDERS_API_CLIENT_SECRET, so Client Components can call the API directly
An unprefixed variable, read only in a DAL module that imports server-only
publicRuntimeConfig in next.config.ts, which keeps it out of the JavaScript bundle
localStorage, written by the login page and sent by the browser on each call
explain: Unprefixed variables stay on the server, and server-only turns an accidental import from a Client Component into a build error. A NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable is inlined into the browser bundle, which publishes the secret; publicRuntimeConfig was removed in Next.js 16.

q: app/products/[slug]/error.tsx exists. Which error does it not catch?
options: An error thrown while rendering page.tsx in the same folder
An error thrown by a nested layout in a subfolder
An error thrown while rendering a Client Component used by the page
An error thrown by app/products/[slug]/layout.tsx
explain: Next.js documents that error.js wraps the page, loading, not-found and nested layouts, but not the layout.js of its own segment. An error there goes to the parent's boundary, or to global-error.tsx for the root layout.

q: An old product page uses getStaticPaths with fallback: 'blocking'. What replaces it in the App Router?
options: An async Server Component without caching, the equivalent of getServerSideProps
A Route Handler in route.ts that returns the list of paths to the build
generateStaticParams, plus dynamicParams for unlisted slugs
A loading.tsx shown during generation
explain: The migration guide maps getStaticPaths to generateStaticParams and the fallback option to dynamicParams; 'blocking' has no direct equivalent because streaming made the difference negligible. Route Handlers replace pages/api, not static paths.

q: An interviewer asks: "Is 'use server' the opposite of 'use client'?" Which answer is accurate?
options: No: Server Components have no directive; 'use server' marks Server Functions
Yes: 'use server' marks a component as a Server Component, the default being client
Yes, but only in Next.js
No: 'use server' marks code that runs once at build time and never per request
explain: react.dev says it directly: a common misunderstanding is that Server Components are denoted by 'use server', but there is no directive for them; the directive is for Server Functions. That is also why a file marked 'use server' exposes callable endpoints.

q: Each call takes about 200 ms and none depends on another. Which change would you ship?
options: Wrap the three functions with React.cache so their results are reused within the request
Mark the page 'use client' so the browser fetches the three in parallel after hydration
Promise.all for product and stock; reviews in a child under Suspense
Add a loading.tsx and keep the code
explain: The three sequential awaits are a server waterfall of about 600 ms; parallel requests cut it to the slowest one, and streaming the optional reviews keeps the LCP content from waiting. React.cache only deduplicates repeated calls, and loading.tsx shows a fallback but leaves the waterfall in place.

q: How many times does fetchCurrentCustomer run in one request?
options: Once: cache recognises that both wrappers point to the same underlying function
Twice: each call to cache creates a new memoized function with its own, separate cache
Zero: cache defers the call until a Client Component actually reads the customer
Once per customer, because the memoized value is shared across their requests
explain: React documents that calling cache with the same function several times returns different memoized functions that do not share a cache, so components must import one memoized function defined at module level. And the cache never spans requests, which rules out the last option.

q: The page renders its header, then a component inside <Suspense> fetches the product and calls notFound() because it does not exist. What does the crawler receive?
options: A 404 status with the not-found UI, since notFound() sets it
A 500 status, because notFound() throws while the response streams
A 410 status, because Next.js knows the product was deleted
A 200 status with the not-found UI and a noindex meta tag
explain: Streaming responses start with 200 and the first chunk fixes the status; Next.js then streams the not-found UI and adds noindex so the URL leaves the index. To return a real 404, check existence in the page before the first Suspense boundary.

q: A returning customer has 3 items in a cart stored in localStorage. What happens on page load?
options: A mismatch: the server renders 0 and the client 3; read storage after mount
It works: the typeof window check is the recommended way to avoid hydration errors
The server throws a ReferenceError on localStorage and the whole page fails to render
React patches 0 into 3 silently
explain: The check runs differently on the server and in the browser, so the first client render differs from the HTML: measured in jsdom, the server sent 0, hydration reported a text mismatch and the badge ended at 3 after a client re-render. The guard avoids the ReferenceError, which is why the code looks safe, but it creates the mismatch.

q: A CMS description renders as <p><p>In stock</p></p> in a Client Component. React renders the same elements on server and client. Why does hydration still fail?
options: React's reconciler refuses nested paragraphs on the client, but accepts them on the server
Next.js minification drops the inner paragraph
The browser's parser closes the first <p> at the second, so the DOM differs
The server escapes the inner paragraph as text, so the client sees different content
explain: Measured in Chromium 156: the markup became <p></p><p>In stock</p><p></p>, so React found a different DOM and reported a hydration error, after warning that a <p> cannot be a descendant of a <p>. The fix is valid markup, such as a <div> wrapper.

q: After the December 2025 advisory (CVE-2025-55182), a colleague says the storefront is safe because it defines no Server Functions. Your answer?
options: Agreed: only apps that expose Server Function endpoints were affected by that advisory
Not necessarily: apps supporting RSC could be vulnerable without them; patch
Agreed: hosting providers blocked the exploit at their edge, so no upgrade is needed
Only the Pages Router parts are affected, so finishing the App Router migration fixes it
explain: The React post states that an app may still be vulnerable if it supports React Server Components even without Server Function endpoints, and that hosting mitigations must not replace an immediate update. Apps without a server or without an RSC-capable framework were not affected.

q: What is wrong with this cached function?
options: Nothing: Next.js adds the cookie value to the cache key automatically for cached functions
The lifetime is too long for a price
getCurrentCustomer must also be wrapped with React.cache for the key to work
Cached functions cannot read cookies, even via a helper: pass the id in
explain: Next.js documents that 'use cache' scopes cannot access cookies() or headers(), and the restriction follows the call stack, failing with next-request-in-use-cache. Passing the customer id as an argument makes it part of the key; nothing is added to the key automatically.

q: The back office calls the storefront's POST /api/revalidate Route Handler after an agent edits a description. A few seconds of stale content are fine, and the handler must not block. Which call?
options: updateTag('product-' + slug) from the handler
revalidatePath('/', 'layout') to clear everything
revalidateTag('product-' + slug, 'max')
cacheLife('seconds') on getProduct instead
explain: revalidateTag with a profile gives stale-while-revalidate and is allowed in Route Handlers; tags invalidate just that product. updateTag is restricted to Server Actions, invalidating the root layout path is far wider than needed, and a seconds lifetime takes the product out of the static shell for every visitor.

q: A candidate says: "fetch in a Server Component is cached by default." Which answer is accurate as of October 2026?
options: True in Next.js 14; not by default since Next.js 15; with Cache Components you cache explicitly with 'use cache'
True in every version: Next.js always caches GET requests made with fetch until a revalidation
False in every version: Next.js has never cached fetch results, only whole rendered pages
True only when Cache Components is enabled, because it caches every fetch made during render
explain: Next.js 15 changed the default: fetch requests and GET Route Handlers are no longer cached by default, and Cache Components (Next.js 16) makes caching opt-in with directives. Cache Components does the opposite of the last option. Stating the version first is the point of the question.

q: What is the vulnerability in this Server Action?
options: It lacks a CSRF token, and Next.js does not check the origin of Server Action requests
No ownership check: any signed-in customer can cancel any order by its id
It should be a GET Route Handler, because cancelling an order twice is idempotent anyway
Throwing on a missing session leaks the stack trace and the message to the customer
explain: Authentication is checked, authorisation of the object is not: the order id comes from the client, so this is an IDOR. Next.js already compares Origin and Host for actions, and production errors from the server reach the browser as a generic message with a digest, so the other options are not the issue.

q: A double click created two orders. A teammate says: "Next.js dispatches Server Actions one at a time per client, so this cannot happen any more." Your answer?
options: Correct: sequential dispatch makes every Server Action idempotent on the server side
Disabling the button while the action is pending is enough; no server change is needed
Call it through Promise.all to merge clicks
Dispatch is client-side; the server does not queue: use an idempotency key
explain: The Next.js docs state that sequential dispatch belongs to the client dispatcher and that the server runs each action as it arrives: a second tab, a retry or a replayed POST still creates a second request. Only a key stored by the Orders API (M05) makes the retry return the first order.

q: An attacker adds totalCents=1 to the form data of the "Place order" form. What does parsed.data contain (measured with Zod 4.6.7)?
code:
const PlaceOrderInput = z.object({ cartId: z.uuid(), idempotencyKey: z.uuid() });
const parsed = PlaceOrderInput.safeParse(Object.fromEntries(formData));
options: Only cartId and idempotencyKey: keys the schema does not declare are dropped
cartId, idempotencyKey and totalCents: '1', kept as a string
Nothing: safeParse fails because the object contains an unknown key
totalCents: 1, converted to a number, next to the two ids
explain: A Zod object strips keys it does not declare: the measured result held only the two UUIDs. Failing on unknown keys would need a strict object. And the action never reads a price from the client anyway: the Orders API computes the total.

q: The order is created, yet the customer sees "Could not place the order." Why?
options: redirect is forbidden in Server Actions
createOrder throws after the order is saved, because the API answers 201 Created
redirect throws, and the catch swallows it: call it after the try/catch
redirect needs an explicit 303 status argument when it is called in a Server Action
explain: The redirect docs say it throws a control-flow error and must be called outside the try block; here the catch turns a successful redirect into an error message. Redirects are allowed in Server Actions, and Next.js picks 303 itself for form submissions without JavaScript.

q: The back office (a separate Vite app) must notify the storefront after a product edit. Server Action or Route Handler?
options: A Server Action, since both are POST requests and the action id is in the client bundle
A Route Handler: a stable URL for callers other than your own UI
A proxy.ts rule that intercepts the call and invalidates the product before routing
A Client Component calling router.refresh()
explain: Server Actions are referenced by build-specific encrypted ids, meant to be called by your own React UI; another app needs a stable endpoint. A Route Handler exposes POST /api/revalidate, checks a shared secret and calls revalidateTag. A proxy rule only intercepts requests before routing.

q: CI builds one image with NEXT_PUBLIC_PAYMENT_ENV=sandbox; production runs the same image with NEXT_PUBLIC_PAYMENT_ENV=live. What does browser code read?
options: live, because the runtime environment variable always wins
An empty string, because the build and runtime values conflict
Nothing: the container refuses to start when a public value changes
sandbox, because public variables are inlined at build time
explain: Next.js documents that NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the JavaScript during next build and frozen: a single image promoted across environments keeps the build value. Per-environment values must be read on the server at request time. Replacement by an empty string is what happens to unprefixed variables in client code.

q: In production, the Orders API fails while a Server Component renders, and error.tsx displays error.message. What does the customer see?
options: The original message with the full stack trace from the server
A generic message, with a digest you can match against the server logs
The JSON error body that the Orders API returned to the server
An empty string, because server errors are never forwarded to it
explain: Next.js replaces the message of errors forwarded from Server Components with a generic one plus a digest, to avoid leaking sensitive details; the original message reaches the browser only in development. That is why error.tsx should log the error and show a fixed sentence.

q: Which of the shop's screens would you not move to Server Components?
options: The back office orders table: logged in, no SEO, heavy client state
The storefront product page, which must be indexed by Google and paint fast on mobile
The marketing landing pages, which change only when the content team publishes in the CMS
The order confirmation page, which shows one order read from the Orders API
explain: Server Components pay off for SEO, first paint and keeping data access on the server; a logged-in, highly interactive table gains little and already runs well as a Vite SPA with TanStack Query. The other three screens are exactly where a static shell and server data help most.
